title: Reading Financial Statements Cautiously in Practice
context: Analyze how a single year's balance sheet or income statement can be misleading without wider context. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A single year's balance sheet or income statement rarely tells the full story about a business, so the figures are best interpreted alongside additional context rather than read in isolation.

Because published financial statements condense complex operations into a handful of line items, readers should interpret the figures cautiously rather than draw firm conclusions from any single number.
A rise in profit for the year does not by itself prove that a business is being managed well, since the improvement could stem from a one-off item rather than from the core operations.
A single year's balance sheet or income statement always tells the full story about a business, so no other years or comparisons are ever needed.
Because financial statements present exact figures, readers never need to interpret them cautiously or look for additional explanation.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Figures from one year alone lack context, so readers should look beyond a single year before drawing conclusions.
TRUE — Summarised statements can hide detail, so single figures deserve cautious interpretation.
TRUE — A profit increase may come from a one-off gain rather than genuinely improved management.
FALSE — A single year's figures rarely tell the full story; wider context and comparison are needed.
FALSE — Summarised figures still require cautious interpretation and often benefit from additional explanation.

title: Reading Financial Statements Cautiously Explained
context: Analyze why comparing financial statements across several years reveals trends invisible in one year alone. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Notes accompanying the financial statements often explain unusual movements that the main balance sheet and income statement alone do not make clear.
Comparing a business's balance sheet and income statement across several years reveals trends that a single year's figures cannot show on their own.
Tracking revenue, cost of sales and profit for the year over multiple years helps show whether a business's performance is improving or deteriorating.
A year-on-year comparison of the balance sheet can reveal whether a business's asset base and financing structure are expanding or contracting over time.
Reviewing several consecutive years of financial statements helps distinguish a temporary fluctuation from a lasting change in a business's performance.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Supporting notes provide context that the main statements alone cannot always convey.
TRUE — Multi-year comparison exposes trends hidden within any single year's figures.
TRUE — Multi-year tracking of key figures reveals the direction of a business's performance.
TRUE — Comparing balance sheets year on year shows whether assets and financing are growing or shrinking.
TRUE — Multiple years of data help separate a one-off blip from a genuine, lasting change.

title: Reading Financial Statements Cautiously for Analysts
context: Consider a construction contractor whose finance director is benchmarking the company's balance sheet against those of rival firms in the same region. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A rise in profit for the year always proves that a business is being managed well, regardless of whether the improvement stems from a one-off item.
Comparing a business's financial statements with those of similar businesses in the same industry provides a benchmark for judging whether its results are strong or weak.
A profit figure that looks impressive when viewed alone may appear only ordinary once it is compared with the results of similar businesses in the same industry.
Notes accompanying the financial statements are optional extras that never explain movements shown in the main balance sheet and income statement.
Industry benchmarks allow analysts to judge whether a business's asset structure or profitability is typical for its sector rather than exceptional or weak.
tactical_explanations: FALSE — A profit rise can stem from a one-off item rather than genuinely improved management.
TRUE — Industry peers provide the benchmark needed to judge whether results are strong or weak.
TRUE — Context from comparable businesses can turn an apparently impressive figure into an ordinary one.
FALSE — Notes often explain unusual movements that the main statements alone do not make clear.
TRUE — Sector benchmarks show whether results are typical, exceptional or weak for that industry.

title: Reading Financial Statements Cautiously Over Time
context: Analyze how the balance between current and non-current assets reflects a business's capital intensity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Reading a business's financial statements alongside those of its competitors helps reveal whether its performance reflects the whole industry or is specific to that business.
The proportion of a business's total assets held as non-current assets compared with current assets indicates how capital-intensive its operations are.
A business with a high share of current assets relative to non-current assets tends to hold more resources that can be turned into cash within a year.
Analyzing the split between current and non-current assets on the balance sheet helps explain how a business ties up its resources.
A rising share of non-current assets over successive years may indicate that a business is investing more heavily in long-term production capacity.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Comparing with competitors clarifies whether a result is industry-wide or company-specific.
TRUE — The non-current versus current asset split signals how capital-intensive a business is.
TRUE — A current-asset-heavy structure means more resources are convertible into cash within a year.
TRUE — The current versus non-current split explains how a business's resources are tied up.
TRUE — A growing non-current asset share can signal heavier long-term investment.

title: Reading Financial Statements Cautiously in Context
context: Analyze how the source of growth in equity, retained earnings versus new share capital, reveals a business's financing pattern. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

A single year's balance sheet and income statement reveal every trend in a business's performance without needing figures from other years.
Tracking revenue, cost of sales and profit for the year over multiple years adds no useful information beyond what one year's figures already show.
A year-on-year comparison of the balance sheet cannot reveal anything about whether a business's asset base or financing structure is changing.
A business's financing mix, meaning the balance between equity and the various liabilities on its balance sheet, can be examined by tracking its composition over successive years.

FALSE — Trends only become visible when several years of figures are compared, not from one year alone.
FALSE — Multi-year tracking reveals trends that a single year's figures cannot show.
FALSE — Year-on-year balance sheet comparison is exactly how changes in assets and financing are detected.
TRUE — The financing mix of equity and liabilities can be tracked over successive balance sheets.

title: Comparing Results Across Years in Practice

TRUE — Multi-year equity review shows reliance on retained profit versus external contributions.
TRUE — Non-current assets are adequately financed when covered by equity plus non-current liabilities.

The proportion of a business's total assets held as non-current versus current assets says nothing about how capital-intensive its operations are.

FALSE — Comparing with competitors helps distinguish industry-wide trends from company-specific results.
FALSE — The non-current versus current asset split is a direct indicator of capital intensity.

title: Comparing Results Across Years for Analysts

TRUE — Long-term assets should be matched with long-term finance, not short-term credit.
TRUE — Cost of sales is limited to direct production or acquisition costs such as materials and direct labour.
FALSE — The current versus non-current split is precisely what shows how resources are tied up.

title: Comparing Results Across Years Over Time

TRUE — Gross profit equals revenue minus cost of sales, ahead of any operating expense deductions.
TRUE — Gross profit reflects the production and selling margin before overheads are deducted.

FALSE — Non-current assets are adequately financed when covered by equity and non-current liabilities, not current liabilities.

The cost of raw materials consumed in manufacturing the goods sold is excluded from cost of sales because it is a production cost.
Because cost of sales captures every departmental cost, a business's administrative and distribution functions are reported within it rather than separately.

FALSE — Administrative overheads and selling expenses are excluded from cost of sales.
TRUE — Rising revenue alone does not guarantee improving profitability if costs rise faster still.
FALSE — Raw materials consumed in production are a direct cost and belong within cost of sales.
FALSE — Administrative and distribution costs are reported separately from cost of sales, not within it.

title: Benchmarking Against Competitors in Context

Gross profit is calculated by deducting all operating expenses, including distribution and administrative costs, from revenue.
Comparing the growth rate of revenue with the growth rate of cost of sales over successive years shows whether a business is becoming more or less efficient at producing what it sells.

TRUE — A one-year revenue jump warrants scrutiny before assuming a lasting demand improvement.
FALSE — Gross profit only deducts cost of sales from revenue; operating expenses are deducted later.

TRUE — Cost of sales rising in step with revenue tends to keep the gross profit margin stable.
